en: Moved and settled at Ürbüs.
They said, “Bakai has become a raider,”
And I acquired an evil name.
Five hundred households remained,
At Bek-Jailoo, above Besh-Tash,
I, Bakai, remained in hiding.
A great dispute arose and tangled us;
My poor soul fought those six vile ones,
Exchanging fire for twelve years.
I let no soul ascend Besh-Tash,
Broke up its entrance and held a fort,
Held it firmly, letting no one pass.
As I persisted in defiance,
Some sixty champions of Abyke
I shot down by myself.
I climbed to a strong place and settled;
I earned the name of troublemaker,
And acquired an evil name.
Drinking blood, I hardened myself.
Among the many Kyrgyz and Argyn,
I was called Bakai the fugitive.
I slaughtered kin and drank their blood;
I, upright Bakai, drank poison.
Not a soul came to visit,
And I lacked strength against the vile ones.
The young falcon went back to its place,
The wanderer back to his camp;
The harrier went back to its place,
The mixed folk back to their camps.
My poor soul stayed and endured
In the land Khan Manas had found.
Ah, the dogs! The fugitives went to their own kind.
I had no khan to support me,
No one like you, left by my Khan Manas,
No orphan bringing blessings.
Such is this world of shit!
When mountain-like Manas died,
When Bakai came to know torment,
Those coarse dogs gathered,
And raided my caravan at the ford.
From those dogs that swaggered proudly,
My foal, I still have not taken revenge.
They broke up my migration from Talas;
From those strutting slaves,
I still have not taken revenge.
No back on which to bind my belt,
No place in which to hide—
My orphan fled before he was grown.
When you went to Bukhara,
My foal, my wing lost a whole span.
The offspring of a khan's son—
Otherwise, why should he have to flee?
The hostility of dogs in the camp,
The six vile ones' lack of fellowship!
A nobleman's young camel—
Why should he have to flee away,
Carried off to Bukhara?
Such a lack of care among the people!
Now know, my foal,
The hostility of those six vile ones.
When the slaves came in a mass,
When they raided livestock without a master,
Kökcholok remained, and I remained.
My Talas stayed safe;
This soul of mine remained free.
We bound our birch-shafted spears,
And warred for twelve years.
Splitting gallbladders, cutting off heads,
We suffered great torment.
Here I, Bakai, did not die,
Nor did I see the other world.
I suffered sorrow for your sake;
Semetey, did you ever think of me?
I wasted away herding camels.
Twelve years had passed
As I wondered, ‘Will my orphan come?’
And burned with longing for you.
Now God has granted my wish,
And the orphan I awaited has come.
Now listen, orphan,
Lend your ear to what I know:
There is a wrong Kanykei has done,
There are wonders in many places.
My spring that feeds a valley river,
My dear one, found when I was near death,
When the possessions were scattered,
When your poor mother fled,
We would earn blame if we left without seeing it:
The treasury your mother dug
She entrusted to poor me,
And left it in my keeping.
Let us go to your treasury;
From the wealth your father left,
Let us take whatever you desire.”
So saying, Bakai sped away,
Urging his horse toward the blue cliff.
At the bubbling dark spring,
At the plane tree by the spring,
They stopped and offered prayers,
Then passed on farther.
They came to hills on hills,
To hilly passes and ridges.
Taking a shortcut on a narrow path,
And leading Semetey,
At Kapka-Tash, where treasure lay hidden,
Gold and jewels intermingled,
They now passed through Kapka-Tash.
The black cliff mottled gray—
The treasure left in trust—
They reached that treasury.
When he examined his treasury,
A jutting ledge of the gray-mottled cliff
Had been brought down from above,
And toppled toward the cave.
His treasure could not be seen.
The possessions my dear mother Kanykei
Had hidden away—
Where they lay could not be known.
Though he looked, they did not meet the eye;
If brave Bakai had not been there,
Your boy would never have known.
Bakai on Kökcholok led the way
To the cave where stones had poured down.
Lion Bakai, the hero,
Took his spear in hand.
Many jutting stones like little chests,
Heaped sand and black rock—
Khan Bakai made them thud,
And stood pounding at them.
“Oh, my orphan left by Manas,
My dear one whom I take for shelter,
My beloved, left by my khan,
My darling orphan,
Try scattering this sand;
Try opening your cave.”
As Khan Bakai
Spoke thus to the boy,
His forefathers all were khans,
Blessed by Khizr from their roots;
He was the only son of a rooted house.
His earliest fathers all were khans,
Blessed by Khizr from the beginning;
He was the sovereign's only son.
If you ask about his fathers:
Eelikme and Jeldüü, two khans;
From those two khans came Tümön Khan.
Tümön Khan's own son
Was fierce Batyrkan, who rode by night.
From Batyrkan came Böyönkan,
From Böyön Khan came Chayan Khan.
Descended from Chayan Khan,
After him came Balakan.
Bala Khan's son
Was Ogoi Khan, born a hero.
Ogoi Khan's son,
After him, was Karakan.
Descended from Karakan
Was ill-intentioned Jakyp Khan.
Born of Jakyp Khan
Was dark, fierce Khan Manas.
When he reached twelve,
He broke courts and took spoils,
Took twelve cities at a stroke,
And stirred strife across the earth.
Kerki Khan of the Russians,
And Molto Khan of the Chinese—
He warred with both for five years.
Those who came and heeded words,
He subdued with words;
Those who would not accept the faith,
He bound them hand and foot,
Subjected them to hardship and humiliation,
Seized them and laid them low.
Wherever there was resistance,
He used his strength and laid it low.
When Manas reached thirteen,
None remained to answer back.
When he reached fourteen,
He turned and moved like a lion.
The khans who heard his fame
Wept bitterly in their souls;
Their eyes were opened wide.
Manas arose as khan among the Kyrgyz,
And souls departed from his wrath.
No claimant remained to demand payment,
No foe remained to face him.
He found the tamarisk-grown land of Talas,
Found the Argyn and Kyrgyz people.
The precious land of Jeti-Suu—
Pressing on, he made it his land.
The Kyrgyz of Jeti-Suu
He forced to become his people.
His fame was known among the peoples;
Those who heard of Manas burned with grief.
Beijing's Kagan khan—
In his register the name was written.
Born of Sultan Manas, mighty in spirit,
Was Semetey, born renowned.
Once Bakai had found the cave,
The poor orphan born of Manas
Bent his knee to the ground;
From Aktulpar's back
He jumped down and ran.
He struck and pulled with his battle-axe;
Ah, the scoundrel born of Manas
Cleared away the fallen sand.
When he had opened it and looked,
The treasury's mouth appeared.
The orphan left by Manas—
The sight distracted his heart.
As the boy stood looking,
Alas, tears poured from his eyes.
The noble lion, proud as a cock,
The noble hero sobbed and wept:
“Oh Bakai, my support, my khan uncle,
My mother was left besieged,
My treasury was left to plunder.”
Standing sorrowful, Semetey
Looked straight before him.
There was writing on the black stone;
When he read the writing,
There was my dear mother Kanykei's name.
She had had the mouth hollowed out
So a single person could fit,
And the farther part dug out
So six thousand sheep could lie there.
A black rock as large as a hut—
He heaved that black rock over.
That his mother was a sovereign,
The boy Semetey now understood,
And entered the treasury.
When he entered the treasury
And looked to right and left,
Gold and rubies lay mingled.
His dear soul stood amazed.
Countless treasures, worldly wealth—
The treasury my mother
Had sealed securely as a trust,
My valiant mother, ill-fated one—
But that she slaughtered five innocent men,
That brought her an evil name.
Without letting a single person know,
Without letting a single person sense it,
My mother left it as a trust.
Of rubies like reclining camels,
A treasury gathered solely—
While my father Manas lived,
It was wealth amassed in plenty.
Andijan's yellow-mottled cloth with thick weft,
Bukhara's costly black-mottled fabric—
She gathered and packed it all.
So much gold, countless possessions,
She entrusted to her dear Semetey.
‘Let him know my worth,’ she said,
‘Let him suffer no humiliation till he dies;
Let my orphan put it to use.’
